messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mele was a 63-year-old project manager who had spent most of her adult life being the person other people relied on: organized, steady, and able to keep complicated timelines moving. Last year, that sense of herself was shattered by a life-threatening medical crisis that began with what she had expected would be a routine workup and became a terrifying sequence of hospital admissions, invasive procedures, and the real possibility that she might die. What remained most vivid to her was not a clean story she could tell from beginning to end, but moments: the sight of needles being prepared, the clear tubing of a drip beside her bed, the feeling of being pinned in one position while people worked over her body and spoke in urgent voices. Even now she said she “couldn’t put it into words properly.” When the memory came, it did not feel like remembering. It arrived all at once, as if the hospital room were happening again across all her senses, and her body would tense into the same helpless position she had been in during the procedures.

In the months after she was discharged, Mele had come to believe that what happened to her body had permanently altered her life. She felt ashamed of what her body had been reduced to in those rooms, exposed and dependent, and she spoke with bitterness about no longer being able to trust her own body. If it could fail her once so dramatically, she was certain it could do so again without warning. Those beliefs made any reminder of illness feel charged before anything had even happened. A conversation at work about someone’s test results, a relative mentioning a biopsy, or seeing medical equipment during an appointment immediately seemed dangerous to her, not merely unpleasant, because they touched the part of her that believed her body was defective and her life had already been destroyed.

Those same beliefs also seemed to draw the memories closer. When she dwelled on how ruined she felt or on the conviction that her body could not be trusted, the fragmented hospital moments pressed in more forcefully. She would find herself overtaken by the sensory reality of the event and unable to explain it in words, only to feel again the bodily submission and fear of lying still while something frightening was being done to her. And when those memory states took over, they seemed to confirm her worst conclusions about herself: if her body could so instantly become that terrified, frozen body again, then to her it proved that the trauma had marked her permanently and that ordinary life had been taken from her.

Her work as a project manager made the problem hard to contain. In meetings, when colleagues discussed insurance, sick leave, or an employee’s upcoming medical procedure, Mele felt her attention narrow and her body jolt into readiness. She became irritable in ways she did not recognize as herself, snapping at coworkers for small mistakes and struggling to follow conversations once she had been set off. If someone approached from behind and touched her shoulder to get her attention, she reacted with visible alarm. At times the trigger was external and obvious, like passing a clinic area with visible medical equipment during one of her own follow-up visits, but sometimes it was the memory itself that sensitized her to the next reminder; after a reliving episode, even the possibility of medical talk later that day felt unbearable.

The memories and sense of current threat fed each other. When she was already on edge—startling at touch, scanning her surroundings, unable to concentrate—her mind seemed more vulnerable to being seized by the hospital scenes. Then, once the memory became fully real and bodily, her system behaved as though the danger were present now: she grew short-tempered, mentally scattered, and braced against contact. In that state she told herself with increasing certainty that her body was unreliable and that the life she had known was gone. Those conclusions did not calm her; they sharpened her vigilance and made the next reminder hit harder.

By the time she sought help, the pattern had begun to constrict both her marriage and her work. Her husband had become wary of raising even ordinary health topics because conversations could end with Mele angry, withdrawn, or visibly shaken. At work she was frightened by how often she lost track during meetings after a medical reference, and by how unlike herself she felt when touched unexpectedly in the office. What finally brought her in was not only the distress of the memories, but the fear that she was becoming permanently unreachable to the people around her. More than anything, she wanted to know whether she could ever feel safe in her own body again, and whether the hospital would stop happening to her every time something in the present reminded her of it.
